alito-recusal:
The Supreme Court announced Monday that Justice Samuel Alito will not take part in next week's landmark climate case, opening the possibility of a four-to-four split. He gave no reason, according to USA Today's reporting.

The case: the city of Boulder and surrounding county sued in 2018, alleging ExxonMobil and Suncor violated state law by misleading the public about the environmental effects of fossil fuels and should help cover climate-related community costs. The companies deny the allegations and argue local governments cannot use state law for what they call a global issue. The appeal is argued October 5, the first case of the court's new term.

Environmental groups had urged recusal because Alito owns stock in ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, both targeted in similar suits. Alexandra Nagy of Consumer Watchdog said that as a shareholder he had been warned climate-deception suits pose financial risks to his investments. The stock-holdings explanation is an inference from critics, not a confirmed fact.

The history adds texture. Alito recused from the 2023 decision on whether the court should intervene at an earlier stage of the Colorado litigation, and did not participate in the court's 2025 rejection of a similar Hawaii appeal. In May, a court spokeswoman told NBC News that legal counsel had advised recusal was not required because “he does not have a financial interest in any party.” Four months later, he is recusing from the merits argument, with no reason given.

The arithmetic: with a 6-3 bench, one recusal opens a possible 4-4 split. If that happens, the oil companies' appeal fails and Boulder's lawsuit proceeds in the lower courts — but no national precedent is set, leaving dozens of similar suits without a Supreme Court answer. USA Today characterized the stakes as billions of dollars potentially at issue.

The underlying legal question is whether cities and counties can use state law to seek climate-damage costs from oil companies. If municipalities can recover adaptation costs from energy companies, the funding model for climate resilience changes nationwide; if they cannot, taxpayers fund sea walls, stormwater systems, and wildfire response. The direction of the outcome is unresolved.
college-sports:
The U.S. Senate on Monday passed the Protect College Sports Act 77-22, the first federal overhaul of college athlete compensation rules, sending it to the House. The Senate invoked cloture September 24 by 74-25. The official release came from the Senate Commerce Committee, with Reuters reporting the vote.

The bill was written by Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and introduced in June. It creates a federal right to name, image, and likeness compensation, replacing the patchwork of state laws, school policies, and booster-funded collectives that has governed NIL since 2021.

Schools must share a percentage of media rights, ticket sales, and sponsorships with athletes — a revenue-sharing requirement. Agent fees are capped at 5 percent. Scholarships are guaranteed for 10 years after eligibility ends. Division I schools must cover out-of-pocket medical costs for sports-related injuries and illness for five years after eligibility. Schools cannot pull scholarships over injury or poor performance. Athletes may transfer once with immediate eligibility. Football coaches are barred from midseason moves. Schools must maintain a minimum number of women's and Olympic sports.

Cruz, the bill's Republican architect, said on the floor: “The most important part of the bill is bringing order to chaos,” as reported by USA Today. Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) opposed it: “I regret this day... a bill that's going to hurt so many,” citing pressure from civil-rights and labor leaders and concern the bill disempowers athletes by locking in terms they did not negotiate.

The athlete-protection provisions reach into daily life: the 10-year scholarship guarantee, five years of injury medical coverage, and the ban on pulling scholarships over injury or poor performance — aimed at programs quietly pushing out hurt or underperforming players to free roster spots. The women's and Olympic sports minimum tries to prevent football and basketball money from cannibalizing non-revenue programs.

The bill now goes to the House, whose next scheduled legislative session begins November 9, six days after the midterms. Whether the House acts at all is unresolved, especially with a possible post-election power shift. NBC Sports cited an unnamed SI.com source saying there is “0.0 percent chance” the House passes it before the midterms — anonymous, and to be treated as speculation. Cruz's floor remarks, via the Commerce release, said the bill affects more than half a million college athletes.
glp1-pediatric:
A new study finds that nearly one in six children prescribed GLP-1 weight-loss drugs developed a nutritional deficiency within a year, while almost none received nutritional counseling.

The study by Kirk W. Kerr and colleagues — “Nutritional Deficiencies, Complications, and Nutrition Therapy/Counseling in Pediatric Patients Using GLP-1 Receptor Agonists” — was published in the journal Childhood Obesity in 2026 and surfaced in a Medical Dialogues bulletin September 28.

Researchers analyzed national administrative claims data from 2017 through 2022, a database covering more than 100 million patients. They identified 2,031 children aged 10 to 17 who had received GLP-1 medications, had continuous health coverage, and had no previous nutritional-deficiency diagnosis. The continuous-coverage requirement means these are children whose medical records could actually be tracked.

Within one year of starting treatment, 16.8 percent were diagnosed with a nutritional deficiency. Vitamin D deficiency was most common at 12.4 percent. GLP-1 medications reduce appetite and food intake, which may make it harder for some children to obtain essential nutrients — and adolescence is a period of rapid growth when vitamin D, iron, and calcium are particularly important for bone development.

The counseling gap is stark: only 5 percent of the children received nutritional counseling within 30 days of starting treatment; fewer than 25 percent received it within six months. The researchers recommend nutritional monitoring begin when GLP-1 treatment starts, rather than after a deficiency develops.

The limits are stated by the researchers themselves. A retrospective claims-data study finds association, not causation — it cannot prove the medication caused the deficiencies, and children prescribed these drugs may differ from peers in ways the data cannot capture. Further research is needed, in the researchers' words, on how treatment affects nutrition during childhood and on monitoring and prevention approaches. With adolescent GLP-1 use growing, the study frames a practical care gap: a one-in-six deficiency rate within a year, vitamin D the most common gap, and counseling largely absent.
india-upi:
India's Supreme Court declined Monday to block new charges on digital payments, a decision affecting how hundreds of millions of people pay every day.

A three-judge bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, declined to stay the new merchant discount rate framework and issued notices to the Union government, the Reserve Bank of India, and the National Payments Corporation of India, giving them four weeks to respond to a public interest litigation filed by advocate Anjan Datta. The case challenges the Centre's September 14 notification and the framework announced September 15. Reporting comes from TradingView and Moneycontrol.

The framework takes effect October 15, 2026: a 0.4 percent merchant discount rate on specified person-to-merchant UPI transactions above 2,000 rupees (about $21), capped at 300 rupees for transactions of 75,000 rupees and above. It ends nearly six years of fully free UPI — India's unified payments interface, the world's highest-volume instant-payment system and the primary way more than a billion people transact daily.

Exemptions: person-to-person transfers remain free regardless of amount; merchant payments up to 2,000 rupees remain free; merchants receiving up to 1 lakh rupees per month are exempt; essential sectors (railways, telecom, insurance, fuel, agricultural inputs) pay a flat 5 rupees per transaction; capital-market payments (mutual funds, securities, brokers) face 0.02 percent, capped at 300 rupees. The government says roughly 96 percent of person-to-merchant transactions remain unaffected — a self-reported figure, not independently audited.

The Solicitor General told the court that no fee money goes to the government — “merely a service charge levied by aggregators and banks.” The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of amended Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and questioned why UPI above 2,000 rupees is charged while RuPay debit cards keep no-charge protection. The petitioner's claim that costs could eventually be passed to consumers is argument, not fact; officials say merchants cannot pass it on, but the plea notes no disclosed cost studies exist.

The decision is procedural, not final: the court declined to freeze the framework before it takes effect, and the case continues with a four-week response deadline — after the fees have already started. Starting October 15, larger merchant payments carry a small capped fee while everyday transactions stay free. Merchants are weighing whether to refuse UPI for larger sales or split bills to stay under the 2,000-rupee threshold.
measles:
Pennsylvania's measles outbreak has crossed 900 cases, the state's worst resurgence in decades, and officials disagree over how many deaths the virus caused.

Pennsylvania Department of Health data, reported by Reuters on Monday at 18:33 UTC, shows 68 new measles infections since Wednesday, September 23, bringing the total to 903 as of Monday, September 28. Hospitalizations reached 176, up from 164 on September 23 — the hospitalization count rising faster than the case count is the number epidemiologists watch. Lancaster County remains the hardest-hit area; outbreaks concentrate where vaccination coverage is lowest.

Pennsylvania reported four measles-related deaths among unvaccinated residents earlier this month. Governor Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. disagree over how many were directly caused by the virus. The CDC said it was reviewing how it classifies measles-related deaths; the CDC's website now lists one “verified measles death” without confirming where it occurred.

The distinction matters. “Directly caused by the virus” versus “related to the illness” are different classifications, and the classification changes the official count — a death in a measles patient from a secondary complication can be counted either way. The CDC's review means the standard itself is under reconsideration, and the death toll is genuinely unresolved: four reported by the state, one verified on the CDC website, two officials in disagreement.

Nationally, the CDC reports the United States has recorded 3,659 measles cases in 2026 as of September 24. Pennsylvania's 903 is a large share of that national total. Measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000; outbreaks since have been measured in dozens or low hundreds. Nine hundred three cases in one state is a different scale.

The medical facts: measles is a highly contagious viral disease causing fever, rash, and respiratory complications, preventable with the MMR vaccine — 97 percent protection after two doses, among the highest efficacy figures in vaccinology. Every case in this outbreak is, in the medical sense, preventable. The open questions are the death classification and whether the curve bends.
save-database:
Five weeks before the November 3 midterms, the Supreme Court has let states use a revamped federal voter-citizenship database, while the fight over whether it is lawful continues.

On Friday, September 25, the Supreme Court issued an unsigned emergency stay pausing a June 22 ruling by U.S. District Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan (D.D.C.). She had struck down the administration's revamped Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program for voter checks, finding it violated privacy rights and risked wrongly removing voters, according to the Associated Press via the National News Desk.

SAVE was built to check immigration status for benefit eligibility. The revamp expanded it for voter-roll citizenship checks, adding Social Security Administration records and bulk-search capacity by executive order. The unsigned order lets states voluntarily use the expanded database while the appeal proceeds. Voluntary is the operative word: no state is required to use it. The court did not rule on whether the program is lawful; the underlying legality question is undecided and will be litigated past the election.

Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson, Elena Kagan, and Sonia Sotomayor dissented. Jackson warned the database could wrongly flag lawful voters — a concern with a factual anchor. The AP reported that in Travis County, Texas, officials investigated 97 voters flagged by SAVE as apparent noncitizens and found at least 10 percent, likely up to 21 percent, were U.S. citizens. A double-digit false-positive rate on citizenship flags is the difference between a clean roll and a disputed one.

There is a practical limit that matters more than the stay. Federal law bars most states from systematic voter-roll purges within 90 days of a federal election, and the country is inside that window. The AP assesses immediate midterm impact as likely limited; Norm Eisen of Brookings concurred, pointing to the decision's own acknowledgment of the 90-day window. Individual removals, as opposed to systematic purges, can still proceed in many states.

A secondary outlet reported September 28 that a Florida judge also ordered database access for several states, disagreeing with the June ruling, citing PBS and the AP. That could not be verified against a primary source and remains developing. The verified bottom line: the database is usable by states as of Friday under an unsigned stay with three dissents; the June ruling's findings are paused, not overturned; and the Travis County check remains the hard evidence on accuracy — at least one in ten flagged voters was a citizen.
starship:
SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time on Monday, a milestone in the largest rocket ever built — though the flight was cut short by an engine problem.

The 14th full-scale Starship test flight launched Monday from Starbase, Texas, flying the Super Heavy v3 booster. The upper stage reached orbit for the first time; Mission Control announced: “Starship is orbital.” One engine shut down prematurely before orbit, and controllers flew on with the rest. SpaceX has not detailed the cause. Earlier flights proved the booster could return and the ship could survive reentry; in July a Starship was recovered from the Indian Ocean and inspected by hand, and this flight's heat shield was modified based on those findings.

The flight deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites — the next generation, larger and more capable — joining about 11,000 older Starlinks already providing internet service. The planned 10-hour flight (six laps at 170 miles / 275 km, 17,500 mph) was cut short after a couple of laps; Starship splashed down north of Hawaii about three hours after liftoff instead of the planned Pacific site near Chile, tipping over and erupting in flames. SpaceX said the early end was “out of an abundance of caution” over the engine trouble.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX on reaching orbit and “managing every step in a safe, responsible and especially inspirational way” — the agency's public read on a contractor it depends on for the moon program.

The 407-foot (124-meter) rocket is designed to be fully reusable. Next, per SpaceX and Elon Musk: the next Starship may return to the launch pad for a catch by the mechanical arms — Musk gives it even or slightly better odds, his own projection. A reflight is possible by year's end or early next year. A second launch site is nearing completion at Kennedy Space Center; a third is planned for Louisiana. Starship is meant to haul satellites in bulk, phasing out the Falcon 9 within several years.

The NASA thread: Artemis III could fly as soon as next summer — a triple-launch orbital docking exercise between an Orion capsule with astronauts, Jeff Bezos's Blue Moon lander flying first, and Musk's Starship. Artemis IV, the moon landing, is slated for no sooner than 2028, using whichever lander is ready first. Starship reaching orbit is a prerequisite for its role. Reporting: The Hindu BusinessLine (September 29, covering the September 28 flight; photos by Reuters' Steve Nesius), The Hindu's same-day AP account, SpaceX's update, and Isaacman's statement.
